brief.head: A window both ways
brief.text: A crisis widens the Overton window, Ajay Shah said, so good but heretical ideas become doable. Terrible ideas are normalised too, more dangerously in poor countries. {123-C02}

brief.head: Inventing the enemy
brief.text: Carl Schmitt also said politics requires an “other”, Amit Varma noted. Authoritarians name an enemy, play the victim from strength, and use such rhetoric to create crises. {123-C07}

brief.head: Glimpses of economics
brief.text: Playing on *Glimpses of World History*, Amit Varma suggested a title for Ajay Shah’s next book: *Glimpses of Good Economics*. Shah agreed to write letters of his own. {123-J05}

brief.head: When the centre fails
brief.text: Ajay Shah invoked the poem *The Center Does Not Hold* for Weimar Germany, and saw “more than a passing resemblance” in today’s world, with “crazy on both sides”. {123-J10}

brief.head: Rain stops play

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on reform in hard times
lead.head: Never waste a crisis? Fear one
body: India got some outstanding reforms done in 1991, in the middle of an economic crisis. Ever since, Amit Varma said, people have parroted the conventional wisdom that you can only make great, sweeping changes in a crisis.
On Episode 123 of *Everything is Everything*, Varma and Ajay Shah set out to bust that myth.

The belief, Varma said, mistakes correlation for causation. It also commits selection bias, looking at one crisis that ended well and ignoring what crises in general can do, which can be quite disastrous. {#correlation}
Shah put it more bluntly. “I actually want to say this upside down that crises are truly dangerous times,” he said. {123-C01}
## The policy pipeline
A crisis, Shah argued, can only help if the ideas and the people are already in place, built upstream of the policymakers long before. Otherwise it is fully wasted.

Varma, who once believed 1991 happened only because India had no choice, found the real story through his own conversations. From the late 1960s, Manmohan Singh had quietly built a community of thinkers. When the crisis came, Varma said, “everything was in place.” {123-S01}

Shah turned to the thinker John Kingdon, for whom change needs three streams to meet: a problem, policy ideas and the politics. A crisis can bring the problem and the politics. The policy has to be built in peacetime.

The 2012 Nirbhaya case showed what happens otherwise. The problem and the politics came together, but nobody had spent twenty years on the ideas, and the moment produced only some activist-style lawmaking.
## In the wrong hands
Worse, a crisis can help the wrong people. The checks and balances of society break down, Shah said, and in India, an early-stage democracy, they are weak to begin with.

The template, he said, comes from the philosopher Carl Schmitt: the true ruler is one who can suspend the rule of law in a crisis. Indira Gandhi’s Emergency of 1975 came after inflation of 16 per cent in 1974. Hitler used the Reichstag fire to suspend Germany’s constitution.
Even without malice, Shah said, a weak state with low capability can make a crisis worse.
Hence his taxonomy. A crisis without prepared ideas is wasted. In a fragile state it invites authoritarians. In a state of low capability it brings a flood of incoherent measures.
## Work in peacetime

So what should a reformer do? Not wait for a crisis, Shah said, and not engineer one, but make progress every day, with humility. “So fix the roof while the sun is shining, build the community, build the people, chip away, be a bricklayer.” {123-C13}
Varma brought the argument home. A heart scare earlier this year, which left him with a stent, and diabetes before it, both pushed him into reforms of his own lifestyle.

But he could have died, he said, and he had always known what a healthy life looked like. He lacked the discipline to live it. Had India done the right things before, the 1991 crisis would never have occurred.
The metaphor has a flaw, he admitted. A person can respond to a crisis far more coherently than a state, with all its stakeholders and bad incentives.
“It is in peace times that you win the next war by making sure the next war doesn’t happen,” Varma said. {123-S12}

second.label: The 1974 inflation
second.head: Eight going on economist
second.deck: At eight, Ajay Shah saw through Indira Gandhi’s blame game on prices
body: Ajay Shah used to watch Indira Gandhi blame the inflation of 1974 on hoarders and speculators, bad people holding goods. He was eight that year, and he already knew that prices are made by supply and demand.
He was genuinely baffled. She had received “all those beautiful letters”, *Glimpses of World History*, so she must be a smart person. So why, he wondered, was Indira Gandhi so clueless? {123-J04}

Grown up, he understood. It was populism: stoke hatred against the elites, and nobody blames you for messing up monetary policy. {123-S09} That othering, he said, became the full-blown *Garibi Hatao* ideology, and the attacks on privy purses.

quote.text: When I grew up, I understood this is populism. You want to stoke hatred against the elites.

second.caption: Indira Gandhi’s hoarders

third.head: 1,324 press releases later
body: After demonetisation, Ajay Shah said, the RBI released 74 regulations in 50 days. There had been no planning, so it worked things out on the fly, and made a bad situation worse. {#rbi}
During COVID, the Ministry of Health released 1,324 press releases. “What sense does that make?” Shah asked. {123-S10}

To him this was what the economist Lant Pritchett calls premature load bearing. An institution given more than it can carry does not rise to the task; it collapses into organisational rout, and the result is chaos.

The 2013 taper tantrum was another case. Ben Bernanke made some remarks to a journalist, markets swung around the world, and the RBI and the Ministry of Finance, Shah said, turned a medium problem into a much bigger one.
third.caption: the flood of press releases

sections.label: The steelman
sections.head: In praise of disaster
sections.caption: the case for a crisis
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah to steelman the view he would go on to attack. Shah began with a line he attributed to Rahm Emanuel, who he thought was Barack Obama’s chief of staff: a crisis is a terrible thing to waste. {123-J09}

Behavioural psychology lends support, he said. In prospect theory, people take the world around them as their baseline and, being loss-averse, do not want to rock the boat. In a crisis the world seems to be going to hell anyway, so people look at new things.

His example was food. Through the 1950s and 1960s, many people knew what needed fixing, but it was not getting done. Then the kharif crops of 1965 and 1966 failed, India came to the verge of mass starvation, and the United States bailed it out with food grain. {123-S02}
That focused minds. Indira Gandhi and C. Subramaniam pushed high-yielding varieties, fertilisers and irrigation, and India got the Green Revolution.
## The Overton window
But a crisis widens the Overton window, the range of ideas the public will accept, in both directions, Shah warned. Terrible ideas are normalised too.

~ Varma has pushed two windows himself. On freedom, as a tariff and free speech absolutist, the game is long. On podcast length he claims victory: after his ten-hour and twelve-hour episodes, an hour is no longer a deep dive. {123-S11}

quote.text: Well, many terrible ideas are also normalized when you have a crisis and the Overton window is widened.

sections.label: The prerequisites
sections.head: Upstream of the policymaker
sections.caption: the policy pipeline
body: Before action, Ajay Shah said, ideas and people have to be in place, or a crisis is fully wasted.

Helping a policymaker implement what they already want is a noble impulse, he said, but not of essence. Implement everything that a thousand good Indian policymakers want today, and he doubted it would make India much better. {123-C03}

Fresh thinking comes from outside. Shah recalled a storied economics bureaucrat, very good to him personally, who in the run-up to 1991 was “stubbornly unable to see that this is broken”, defending his own legacy. {123-S03}
## Activism and wonkery

After Nirbhaya, Shah wrote a blog post, *Activism and wonkery are the yin and yang*. {123-R11} Shouting on the streets helps, he said, but real systems have many moving parts, and someone must have simulated them in their mind.
Social media, he added, has produced many more activists, but not more of those people.

~ It takes patience. Shah, Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi finished the first fully worked-out GST proposal in 2003; the first move towards a complete GST came in 2016. “It takes five hundred seminars and conferences to argue about the GST,” he said. {123-S05}

quote.text: If you don’t have all that wonkery, then all the activism of the world is pointless.

sections.label: Chaos is a ladder
sections.head: The true ruler’s moment
sections.caption: Carl Schmitt’s true ruler
body: Ajay Shah wrote “chaos is a ladder” in *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar, Amit Varma said, only to find the line was also in *Game of Thrones*. {123-J03}

In a crisis, Shah said, the norms that restrain power stop working, and a certain kind of policy entrepreneur uses the madness to do very bad things. India, he noted, is only 80 years old as a democracy. {#democracy}
He cited Carl Schmitt, a philosopher who played a role in the emergence of the Nazis, for whom the true ruler is one who can suspend the rule of law in a crisis.
## From inflation to Emergency
Shah traced the 1975 Emergency back to the 1971 war, an enormous fiscal problem, and to 1974, when inflation reached 16 per cent. “Inflation tears the society apart,” he said. {123-C08}
The JP Narayan movement followed, buses were burned, and Indira Gandhi, a “true ruler”, suspended the rule of law. {123-S06}
In Germany, a hyperinflation after the First World War came first, and Hitler later used the Reichstag fire to suspend the constitution.
~ Monetary economists, Shah said, should be held responsible for such disasters, as for the good done since inflation targeting. Varma added the bad leaders who overrule them.

quote.text: Indira Gandhi was a true ruler. Who suspended rule of law in that time of crisis.

sections.label: Weak states
sections.head: Malice, or just muddle?
sections.caption: malice and incompetence
body: Amit Varma told Ajay Shah he loved his beard, then offered him a razor: Hanlon’s. Never attribute to malice, it says, what can be adequately explained by stupidity. {123-J06}

Malice, Shah said, does the most harm where checks and balances are weak. Hitler destroyed the Weimar Republic, an early-stage democracy still figuring out the basics. The United States, a better democracy, saw more limited depredations after 9/11.

He told a story from Jim Comey, then at the top of the US national security establishment, who rushed by car to a hospital to brief a desperately ill official before something bad was done about a mass surveillance programme. {123-S08}
In a fledgling democracy, Shah said, most of us would just bow our heads and go along.
## Giants and pygmies
Then there is incompetence. “Government is the power of giants given to pygmies who are trying to respond on a day to day basis on a crisis,” Shah said. {123-C09}

~ On demonetisation, Shah said a more capable state would have planned it better, though he did not support it. Varma went further: “A more competent state would never have done something so daft and idiotic as demonetisation.”

quote.text: You need those people, you need those amazing people who will stand up and fight for the rule of law

sections.label: Incrementalism
sections.head: No French Revolutions, please
sections.caption: Popper and the British way
body: A good country, Ajay Shah said, makes progress every day, and that progress comes from incrementalism: thinkers criticise the status quo, their ideas become mainstream and slowly percolate to policymakers.

He drew on the philosopher Karl Popper, who separated utopian from incremental social engineering. Grand schemes, like collectivising all the farms of the USSR, generally lead to a terrible mess. {123-C11}
“Sad is a country that needs a hero. Sad is a country that needs a crisis,” he said. {#sad}
## Britain against France

The French Revolution tore society down, Shah said, and set France back for many years. Britain left monarchy for liberal democracy incrementally. Its one critical milestone came when Republicans led by Cromwell cut off the head of Charles I; Parliament’s power grew gradually, and Britain became the most successful country in the world.

Closer to home, he lived through the reform of India’s equity market from 1992 till about 2007, a collaboration of the finance ministry, SEBI, NSE and academics, driven by data and research. {#equity}
~ Both hosts call themselves conservative in Edmund Burke’s sense: not against change, but humble about a complex world in which every step has unintended consequences. {123-C12}

quote.text: I think both of us are liberal in our ends, conservative in our means.

sections.label: The lessons
sections.head: Bricklayers, not saviours
sections.caption: how crises go wrong
body: Ajay Shah ended with a rough taxonomy. Without prepared ideas, a crisis is useless. In a fragile state, would-be autocrats declare themselves the true ruler. In a state with low capability, the result is “a hundred incoherent policy measures”.

Coherence, he said, means understanding the world and finding one strategy for disparate problems. Practical people, solving each problem expediently, produce actions that make a mess with each other. {123-C10}
## Humble, twice

The reformer’s job is to work in peacetime, Shah said: not to wait for a crisis or engineer one, but to lay one brick at a time. He asked for humility twice, because none of us knows the world, and because we must admit when the evidence shows we were wrong. {123-C13}

Amit Varma said his own heart scare and diabetes came because he lacked the discipline for a healthy life he knew about. But a person responds to a crisis far better than a state, with its moving parts and stakeholders.
~ Shah closed by reading Max Weber: politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards, and those who are neither leaders nor heroes must arm themselves with steadfastness of heart. {#weber}

quote.text: Coherence is an intellectual’s word. It is a philosopher’s word.

side.boxTitle: A line before Game of Thrones
side.boxText: Ajay Shah first set out the idea that crises are ladders for the wrong people in *In Service of the Republic*, his book with Vijay Kelkar, which Amit Varma calls Shah’s “fine book”. {123-R01}

contQuote.text: The problems are upstream. You need to change the ideas, you need to change the imagination, you need to build a cadre of people who are upstream of the policymakers

stories.caption: the long road to 1991
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the people who prepared India’s 1991 reforms
stories.head: The baton was passed long before
body: Amit Varma used to think the 1991 reforms came about only because of the balance of payments crisis: in that moment the government had no choice but to reform, though it did not really want to.

Several episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen* and *Everything is Everything* changed his mind. The story, he found, started much earlier, and in that long arc Manmohan Singh is an even greater hero than one would think.

From the late 1960s, Singh was building a community in silent ways. He asked Vijay Kelkar to come back to India in the early 1970s, and Montek Singh Ahluwalia in the late 1970s. It was not exactly an organised effort, Varma said, but it peopled the ecosystem with interesting thinkers.

From the late 1970s, as Ahluwalia described in his conversation with Varma, a bunch of people, many of them inside government, thought quietly about how to make India better. They picked their battles, and did not fight losing ones that could cost them their place.
In 1990, Varma said, Ahluwalia came out with the famous M document, “a work of legend”, which contained much of what was done a year later. {#mdoc}
“So when the ninety one crisis happened, everything was in place,” he said. Nobody was floundering; the body of work was there. {123-S01}

~ Ajay Shah compared it to a relay. We see the last ten seconds of the runner carrying the baton across the line and think, wow, you did it. But the baton had passed through many earlier stages of the policy pipeline.
stories.why: A crisis can open a window, but it cannot fill it. In 1991 the problem and the politics met a policy stream that patient people had spent fifteen or twenty years preparing. {123-C04}

stories.start: Let me take a contrast, which is the opposite of this story
stories.end: other than some activist type lawmaking, which doesn't move the needle
stories.caption: the wasted Nirbhaya moment
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on what came of public outrage in 2012
stories.head: Outrage without a blueprint
body: In 2012, the horrific Nirbhaya rape case in Delhi brought the problem and the politics together, two of the three streams in John Kingdon’s framework, Ajay Shah said. Manmohan Singh and Montek Singh Ahluwalia wanted to use the moment to reform the criminal justice system.

But the policy leg was not ready. Nobody had spent twenty years building people, documents, books, seminars and conferences, and an interconnected picture of how the parts fit together. “None of this can be hatched in a hurry,” Shah said.
“A crisis is a terrible thing to waste, and the Nirbhaya crisis was wasted,” he said. It produced only some activist-style lawmaking, which did not move the needle. {123-S04}
~ Shah had told the story before, in the hosts’ episode *The Long Road to Change*.
stories.why: Public outrage and political will are not enough. If nobody has worked out the ideas in calm times, the window closes with nothing to show for it. Activism, Shah argued, needs wonkery. {123-C05}

stories.start: Similarly, I think after the 911 attacks, there was a hawkish piece
stories.end: given the state a comprehensive ability to snoop on all of us
stories.caption: the 9/11 wish list
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the laws that rode in after 9/11
stories.head: Whoosh, and it was law
body: For a long time, Ajay Shah said, a hawkish part of the United States national security establishment had been nursing authoritarian ideas: the Patriot Act, countering the financing of terror, anti-money laundering and the FATF, which in India means the Prevention of Money Laundering Act and the Enforcement Directorate.
In normal times, he said, principled lawmakers in the Senate and the House of Representatives would have debated such things and refused them as authoritarianism.
“And then came the 9/11 attacks and like whoosh, within weeks all this stuff got through,” Shah said. {123-S07}
~ By and large, he said, every piece was a bad idea. Tracing money flows has never disrupted a terrorist plot; all it has done is build a mass surveillance system in finance.
stories.why: This is the 1991 story with the sign flipped. Bad ideas can also wait in the pipeline, and a crisis lets them through as readily as good ones: terrible ideas, too, are normalised. {123-C02}

stories.start: So I want to bring this to the realm of the personal
stories.end: because individuals can react much better in a crisis than a state
stories.caption: his heart scare
stories.kicker: Amit Varma takes the argument to his own health
stories.head: The patient who knew the cure
body: Earlier this year Amit Varma had a heart scare and got a stent. Before that came diabetes, which he reversed through diet. Both crises pushed him into reforms of his own.

He could have died, he said, and he had always known what a healthy life looked like. He lacked the discipline to exercise every day, do resistance training, avoid sugar and sleep properly. Had he lived that way, neither crisis would have come.

Countries are the same: had India done the right things before 1991, that crisis would never have occurred. “It is in peace times that you win the next war by making sure the next war doesn’t happen,” he said. {123-S12}
~ But the metaphor is flawed, he said. A person responds to a crisis far more coherently than a state, full of stakeholders and bad incentives.

quote.text: A crisis is not to be wished.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah found the analogy remarkable, and hoped we can all turn a personal crisis into a moment of reinvention. {#analogy}

quiz.q: Which two harvests failed back to back, bringing India close to mass starvation?
quiz.a: The kharif crops of 1965 and 1966; the United States sent food grain.

quiz.q: According to John Kingdon, which three streams must come together for meaningful change?
quiz.a: A problem stream, a policy stream and a politics stream, all at once.

quiz.q: Who, by Amit Varma’s account, came out with the famous M document in 1990?
quiz.a: Montek Singh Ahluwalia; it held much of the reform done a year later.

quiz.q: What, by Ajay Shah’s account, did Carl Schmitt say marks the true ruler?
quiz.a: The ability to suspend the rule of law in a time of crisis.

quiz.q: How many years passed between the first worked-out GST proposal and the first real move?
quiz.a: Thirteen: the report was done in 2003, and the move came in 2016.

quiz.q: Whose razor did Amit Varma hand Ajay Shah, and what does it say?
quiz.a: Hanlon’s: never attribute to malice what can be adequately explained by stupidity.
